notes.b: Saving means setting aside part of your income for future use instead of spending it, and it takes planning, such as a budget or paying yourself first. A household that saves is better prepared for what life brings.
points: Saving reduces financial worry and gives the household security against unexpected costs, because there is money to fall back on.
A savings fund covers emergencies, such as job loss, illness or an urgent repair, so the household does not have to borrow.
Regular saving allows the household to plan for expensive items or events, such as a holiday, a car, education, a wedding or a deposit for a home, without using credit.
Saving avoids the need for loans and credit agreements, and so avoids the interest charged on them.
Money held in a suitable scheme earns interest (the payment a bank or other institution makes for holding your money) and grows over time.
Saving for retirement means the household has an income to live on once work stops.
Saving sets a good example for children and builds a sound financial reputation for the family, as well as independence.
Teenagers who save regularly gain financial independence, build a habit, gain security, can reach future goals and avoid credit.
notes.tip: Reasons for saving are asked as short lists. Give security, an emergency fund, avoiding credit and interest, planned purchases, earning interest and setting an example for children, and for teenagers add independence and the saving habit.

notes.b: How long you plan to save for decides what kind of scheme suits you, because the two aims need different things from an account.
points: Short-term saving, for an emergency or a planned spend within a year, needs easy access, so the money can be reached when it is needed.
Long-term saving, for retirement or a house, can accept restricted access in return for higher interest, because the money is not needed soon.
Higher interest generally means less access or more risk, so a saver always gives something up for a better rate.
notes.tip: Do not call a scheme the best without saying which criterion you mean. Higher interest generally means less access or more risk.

notes.b: Banks and building societies offer several kinds of savings account. They differ mainly in how quickly you can reach your money and how much interest you earn in return.
points: A current account is for everyday spending, not for saving.
Demand deposit account: money can be withdrawn on demand (instantly), so it suits short-term saving and an emergency fund, although the interest is low.
Notice account: withdrawals require a set period of notice, and the interest paid is usually higher than on a demand deposit account, because the institution can plan around when money leaves.
Term deposit (fixed-term deposit): money is locked away for an agreed period at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually reduces or loses the interest, or is refused.
Regular saver account: a fixed monthly deposit is made into an account that pays a higher rate in return for regular saving.

notes.b: State Savings products are run by the National Treasury Management Agency and sold through An Post, the Post Office. Because the State stands behind them, they are among the safest places to save.
points: Instalment saving scheme: a fixed amount is saved each month over a set period, and the money is then left to earn interest for a further period.
Savings certificates: a fixed-term product paying interest higher than an ordinary deposit account, with interest reduced if the certificate is cashed in early.
Savings bonds: a fixed-term product, so the money is tied up for the term in return for a better return. Early withdrawal reduces or removes the interest earned.
Prize Bonds give a chance to win prizes rather than earning interest.
Returns on fixed-term products and instalment savings are not subject to DIRT or income tax, which means the saver keeps the whole return.
State Savings are backed by the State, so there is no loss of capital (the money you put in).
notes.tip: Name State Savings or An Post certificates, bonds and instalment savings as schemes, not an old Post Office deposit account. Do not say State Savings fixed-term products have DIRT.

notes.b: A credit union is a different kind of saving institution, owned by the people who save in it rather than by outside shareholders.
points: A credit union is a member-owned, non-profit co-operative serving a local or work-based community (a common bond), and its share and saver accounts are run for its members.
Members can usually save small amounts regularly, often by payroll deduction, which suits a low-income family.
Credit union shares earn a dividend, not interest, paid at the end of the year if the credit union can afford it, so the dividend is not guaranteed.
Members with a savings record find it easier to qualify for a low-cost credit union loan.
Credit union deposits are protected by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme.
notes.tip: Say dividend, not interest, for credit union shares, and remember it is not guaranteed.

notes.h: Other ways of saving or investing
notes.b: Money can also go into products that aim for a higher return, but these carry risk and are not the same as saving.
points: Shares and investment funds, pensions (PRSA, occupational pension, AVCs) and property can give a higher return, but their value can fall.
They are not suited to an emergency fund, because the money may be worth less when it is needed.
Equity-linked products risk loss of capital, whereas savings keep capital safe.
notes.tip: Saving is not the same as investing: savings keep capital safe, while investments can lose it.

notes.h: Savings security and the Deposit Guarantee Scheme
notes.b: Before choosing where to save, the household needs to know how safe the money is if an institution fails.
points: The Deposit Guarantee Scheme protects deposits in banks, building societies and credit unions authorised in Ireland, up to a limit of 100,000 euro per person per institution.
State Savings are backed by the State, so their security does not depend on a guarantee limit.
Investment funds and shares in companies are not covered by the Deposit Guarantee Scheme, so they can lose value.

notes.b: No scheme is best on every count. A saver compares schemes against a set of criteria and picks the one that fits the household's need.
points: Security: how safe the money is, shown by a State or deposit guarantee, the stability of the institution, and the risk of loss with investments.
Interest: the rate paid, whether it is fixed or variable, and how often it is paid.
The annual equivalent rate (AER) shows the yearly return including the effect of compounding, so different schemes can be compared fairly.
Compounding means interest is paid on earlier interest, so a longer-term deposit grows faster than the simple rate suggests.

Access: how quickly and at what cost money can be withdrawn (instant, notice or fixed term), whether penalties apply, and whether the account is by branch or online, with its opening hours and location.

Tax: Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT) is deducted from interest on most bank, building society and credit union deposits before the saver receives it, while State Savings fixed-term products are exempt. Net return matters, not only the headline rate.
Other factors: minimum or regular deposit, fees, convenience, and whether the scheme suits the family's goal and income. A low-income family needs small deposits and easy access.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to explain security, interest rate, access and tax, each linked to the saver's need. DIRT is a tax on interest, so do not say all savings are taxed. Explain compounding or AER only briefly.

notes.h: Matching a scheme to a need
notes.b: The criteria only help once they are tied to what the household is saving for, so a good answer links the purpose to a scheme.
points: Emergency fund: a demand deposit or credit union share account, because money must be reachable at once.
Holiday within a year: a demand or notice account.
Long-term lump sum: a term deposit or State Savings fixed term, because the money can be locked away for higher interest.
Regular small amounts: a credit union, regular saver or instalment savings.
Purpose: short-term access suits emergencies, and longer-term schemes suit planned spending.
notes.tip: When recommending a scheme for a family, name the institution and scheme type, say how interest is paid, how easy access is and what tax applies, and give a reason it suits the family. A single account with one reason can be enough where the question asks for that.

keyTerms.definition: A bank or credit union account from which money can be withdrawn on demand, usually with low interest.
A deposit account that requires a set period of notice before money can be withdrawn.
Money locked away for an agreed fixed period at a fixed rate, with interest lost or reduced on early withdrawal.
A fixed-term Post Office savings product with interest higher than a deposit account, reduced if cashed in early.
A savings account in a member-owned credit union, on which an annual dividend is paid.
The yearly interest rate including the effect of compounding, used to compare savings schemes.
A tax deducted from interest on most bank and credit union deposit accounts before the interest is paid.
Earning interest on both the original sum saved and the interest already added to it.

factCards.definition: Reduces financial worry; provides for emergencies; avoids loans and credit; can earn interest.

factCards.term: Four factors to weigh when choosing a savings scheme
Three types of bank saving account
factCards.definition: Demand deposit, notice and term deposit accounts.

questions.prompt: Name one savings scheme suited to a family saving for a holiday within the next year, and explain how it meets the family's need for access to money.
questions.model: A named scheme such as a demand deposit account or a notice account. Access: a demand deposit account allows withdrawal on demand, so the money is available when the holiday is booked; a notice account needs notice to be given before money can be withdrawn. The scheme earns interest on the savings while they build up. A term deposit would lock the money away and reduce access.

questions.prompt: Compare a bank deposit account, a Post Office savings certificate and a credit union share account as savings schemes for a family, using security, interest, access and tax. Explain which of them would suit a family building an emergency fund.
questions.model: Security: each is a secure place to save, with protection of deposits depending on the institution and any State guarantee. Interest: the savings certificate pays more than an ordinary deposit account but is reduced if cashed in early; the credit union pays a dividend on savings; the bank account pays interest that depends on the account type. Access: the bank demand deposit and the credit union account allow withdrawal, while the certificate is locked for a term. Tax: interest on bank and credit union deposits is subject to DIRT, while savings certificate interest is tax free. A demand deposit or credit union account suits an emergency fund because the money can be reached quickly.
